⚠ Not financial advice.
  • This dashboard is an educational market-monitoring tool, not professional investment research or a recommendation to buy or sell.
  • Data may come from FRED downloads, historical sources, manual entries or AI-assisted research. Figures can be delayed, incomplete or drawn from different observation dates. Local update times record saves or checks, not market observation times.

  • Verify all figures, dates and sources independently before making investment decisions.

Score Bands
📊 Systemic Risk Regime Matrix — Maximum 50 Points
SCORE BAND REGIME LABEL PORTFOLIO REVIEW FOCUS MARKET ENVIRONMENT CHARACTERISTICS
0–4 Normal Risk Review normal allocation Few tracked indicators currently cross the dashboard’s stress thresholds. This does not rule out losses; review allocation against your objectives and risk limits.
5–9 Correction Risk Monitor emerging risks Some indicators suggest emerging macro or technical pressure. Monitor persistence and check the dates and quality of the underlying data.
10–15 Systemic Stress Review exposure and hedges Several tracked indicators suggest stress across markets. Review concentration, leverage and liquidity; the score alone does not determine a trade or a suitable hedge.
16–22 High Stress Review stress plan More indicators meet elevated-stress thresholds. Review your stress plan and exposure to adverse moves; confirm whether signals persist.
23–30 High Risk Review stress plan Many tracked indicators meet stress thresholds. Consider downside scenarios and liquidity requirements; this score does not establish panic or a particular level of asset correlation.
31–50 Systemic Risk Review liquidity needs A high concentration of tracked stress signals warrants closer review of credit, volatility and market participation. It does not prove a credit freeze, predict a crash, or identify capitulation.

⚡ Quick Paste Update- copy and paste this to your AI

Generate a paste-ready line of exactly 39 comma-separated numeric values in the following order. Use completed-session data only for scoring. Start with the latest verified final trading-session observations and the latest published FINRA debt month; if a series is delayed or inaccessible, follow the verified-data and best-estimate fallback rules below. For USDJPY momentum use (latest FX session close / close 3 FX trading sessions earlier − 1) × 100, from one consistent source. Use reported ^GSPC volume consistently; average the preceding 20 sessions excluding the current session. Debt changes compare the same series with 12 and 3 months earlier. Use the latest data and provide evidence-based best estimates for unresolved fields as described below; never present estimates as verified facts:

VIX, VIX 1D %, VIX 5D %, HY OAS, HY OAS 5D bp change, HY OAS 20D bp change, BBB OAS, 10Y Yield, 10Y 20D bp change, S&P vs 50DMA, S&P vs 200DMA, WTI, WTI 20D %, MOVE, USDJPY, Breadth % >50DMA, Breadth 20D change, VIX 3M-1M spread, S&P 500 close, Margin debt reference month (YYYYMM), FINRA margin debt (USD million), Margin debt YoY %, Margin debt 3M change %, S&P reported volume, Prior 20-session volume average, S&P 500 daily change %, USDJPY 3-session change %, S&P 500 session high, S&P 500 session low, Nasdaq Composite close, Nasdaq 100 close, Latest of the three CP/Treasury observation dates (YYYYMMDD), 90-day AA financial CP rate (%), 90-day AA nonfinancial CP rate (%), 3-month Treasury bill rate (%), Equity session date (YYYYMMDD), Financial CP observation date (YYYYMMDD), Nonfinancial CP observation date (YYYYMMDD), Treasury bill observation date (YYYYMMDD)
Suggested source webpages and calculation checks (included in Copy prompt)

Best-estimate fallback (requested): First seek verified data using the sources and checks below. If verification remains incomplete after reasonable alternate-source checks, provide the best defensible estimate and include it in the complete 39-number paste-ready line rather than withholding the line solely because a value is provisional. This exception applies to the 35 market fields only; the four dates must be actual sourced observation dates, never estimates. It applies where there is a credible numerical basis, and takes precedence over strict verification requirements below for those estimated fields. Prefer a credible same-instrument dated observation, then a transparent calculation from sourced endpoints or a clearly disclosed observation-count assumption. For completed sessions, a provider-reported historical value whose finality is not independently confirmed may be used provisionally; do not use a currently unfinished session. For FX source conflicts, select one credible provider and recompute both the level and momentum using its consistent daily convention. For WTI, an uncertain intermediate publication count may be estimated using verified endpoint prices and an explicit count assumption; never substitute futures for spot. For incomplete calculation windows, disclose every estimation method and the actual coverage; never call a shortened window an exact 50/200-session average or a 20-session change. Preserve same-date groups and instrument identity; do not average conflicting feeds, reuse an old change with a new endpoint, or use zero as a missing-value substitute. Keep monthly debt on its latest published reference month and each CP/Treasury rate on its own latest verified observation date, with individual stale labels. Before the numeric line, label the whole row "Provisional best-estimate row" if any field is estimated and list each affected field number/name, value, source date, assumption, reason and confidence. Distinguish verified current, verified older, provisional reported and estimated values in the source table. Do not fabricate source observations or claim full verification. Only withhold the complete line if a field has no defensible numerical basis even after these fallbacks; identify that field plainly.

Newest verified data for every field: Use the newest verified completed-session observation for every market level and the newest published reference month for monthly data. Recalculate each return, spread and average against its updated endpoint. Do not hold a verified newer level back merely because a comparison calendar or related historical window is unavailable. First use the specified market-session calculation. If calendar ambiguity alone prevents a daily lag calculation, use the same series 5 or 20 published daily observations earlier (3 for FX), as applicable: sort unique dated numeric observations, count unchanged publisher-reported dates, exclude blank/n.a. records and duplicate dates, and never invent prices. Clearly label this fallback as an observation-based calculation, with both dates, values and observation count; do not describe it as an exact trading-session change. WTI always uses its published-observation rule below. For moving averages use exactly 50/200 verified daily closes including the newest close; for volume use exactly 20 preceding verified daily volumes excluding the current session. An incomplete download is not permission to skip missing records or shorten a window: seek another complete source. If any derived metric still cannot be verified, retain the newest verified level and apply the best-estimate fallback, explaining the calculation and uncertainty before the numeric line. Preserve matched dates for OHLC/volume and VIX/VIX3M. For CP/Treasury rates, use each series’ latest verified observation independently and preserve all three dates; do not require a common date. FINRA changes still use exact 12- and 3-month comparisons. This newest-data rule overrides older-observation fallback instructions below. Clearly identify methodology changes when comparing with saved history.

Source priority: Check the direct publisher first: Cboe for VIX/VIX3M, US Treasury for the 10-year constant-maturity par yield, EIA for Cushing WTI spot, Nasdaq for its index closes, ICE for MOVE and the exact ICE BofA HY/BBB OAS indexes, the Federal Reserve for CP rates, and FINRA for margin debt. Prefer a verified official downloadable history. If direct data is inaccessible, requires an unavailable subscription, or lacks a complete history window, use FRED or the listed alternate for the exact same series. Compare observation dates, not webpage update times. Retain Yahoo-reported ^GSPC OHLC/volume consistently. Never substitute a different instrument merely because its quote is newer.

Completed-session data only for scoring: Prefer verified final observations for completed sessions. Exclude live, intraday, pre-market, after-hours and unfinished daily candles. Provisional historical observations for completed sessions are allowed only under the best-estimate fallback and must be labelled before the line. Verify the provider's session date, closing time and timezone; a retrieval timestamp after the close alone does not establish that a quote or volume is final. For USDJPY, use the provider's completed daily FX session and the same session convention throughout its history. For Treasury yields, CP rates, WTI spot and margin debt, use the latest officially published daily observation or monthly report, not a live proxy. If a newer quote is unfinished, use the latest completed observation for that field or required same-date group. If only finality verification is incomplete, apply the best-estimate fallback. A missing calculation window alone must not roll back a verified newer level; apply the newest-data rule above. Do not include intraday quotes in the 39-value line.

Verify instrument identity and price consistency: Check the returned symbol, instrument description, units and source methodology, especially for MOVE. If the symbol and description disagree, independently corroborate the exact series and dated close before using it; a matching ticker alone is insufficient. For any OHLC record, require low ≤ open ≤ high and low ≤ close ≤ high on the same session and price basis. Reject inconsistent records, including USDJPY closes outside their daily range; do not repair or estimate them. Try another verified source for the same instrument; reject invalid records and use the newest valid completed observation for the affected field or required same-date group.

CP and breadth verification: Verify CP and breadth claims before interpreting them. Cross-check Federal Reserve H.15 https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/h15/ against the daily AA financial and AA nonfinancial 90-day columns at https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/cp/rates.htm and FRED DCPF3M/DCPN3M/DTB3. Record the observation date and category for each rate; never mistake nonfinancial for financial CP, weekly averages for daily rates, or a release date for a common observation date. An n.a. remains missing. Use the latest individually verified observation for each of the three rates, even when their dates differ. Retain each actual observation date and flag each rate older than seven calendar days. Never roll a newer rate back to force a common date. Label spreads from different dates as asynchronous comparisons, not same-session funding spreads. CP scoring uses BOTH spreads: 0 points only when financial-minus-nonfinancial is below 25 bp AND financial-minus-Treasury is below 50 bp; 2 points if either threshold is reached, replaced by 3 at 50/100 bp respectively. For breadth, verify a dated completed-session S&P 500 percentage above its 50-day average and the same-series value exactly 20 equity sessions earlier; compute the difference in percentage points. Sector breadth, 200-day breadth and live quotes cannot replace this input. Treat MacroMicro sector charts only as supplementary evidence with verified series definitions, dates and values. A reading above 35% does not cross a below-35% trigger. Separate a one-session decline from a confirmed trend reversal or acceleration; those require a comparable time series. Do not claim mega-cap technology exclusively supports an index without dated constituent-weight/contribution evidence.

Source verification record: For every indicator group, provide its exact series/provider, source URL, observation date or reference month, completed-session/publication status, and verification status (verified current, verified older, provisional reported, estimated, or unavailable). Include dated endpoints and values for rolling changes, and the window dates and session count for averages. Separate verified data from interpretation and unverified quoted claims. A previous AI response is not source evidence. For MOVE, prefer ICE end-of-day data; if access is unavailable, require independent dated corroboration of the exact MOVE series whenever fallback metadata conflicts with its symbol. Do not carry an unresolved MOVE quote into a supposedly verified numeric line. Try an older independently verified observation; if none is available, apply the best-estimate fallback only with defensible evidence for the exact instrument. An unresolved instrument mismatch alone is not a basis for an estimate. Never use zero as a missing-value substitute.

Recheck revisions: Retrieve recent history afresh on every request, especially Yahoo ^GSPC reported volume. Prefer the provider's latest verified historical observations over earlier saved downloads when a revision is confirmed. Recalculate all affected returns, moving averages and the preceding 20-session volume average from that history. If feeds disagree for the same date, resolve the discrepancy with dated historical data rather than choosing whichever value is newer or larger. Mention material revisions in the freshness note.

Use the calendar for each market: Count sessions using the relevant market calendar, not calendar days or a universal weekday count. Use the US equity calendar for equity, VIX and breadth windows; Treasury/SIFMA bond-market sessions for Treasury yields and HY spread changes; the published-observation convention below for WTI; and the FX provider's daily session convention for USDJPY. Check bond holidays such as Columbus Day and Veterans Day even when stocks trade. For exact session-based calculations, a holiday carry-forward or month-end non-trading index observation is not an extra trading session. If calendar ambiguity remains, use and disclose the published-observation fallback specified above; WTI always uses its published-observation rule below. For completed-session scoring, use the latest verified trading-session close and count the specified lag from it, identifying excluded non-trading observations in the freshness note. Never mistake a missing trading-session observation for a holiday.

Browse these sources and verify the dates, units and completed-session status. If a page has missing observations, try its official download or the alternate source; do not skip a missing trading session when calculating a change or average.

  • Direct Cboe VIX dashboard; use a verified final close, not the live index: https://www.cboe.com/us/indices/dashboard/vix/
  • Direct Cboe VIX3M dashboard; use the same completed session as VIX: https://www.cboe.com/us/indices/dashboard/VIX3M/
  • Direct US Treasury daily par yield curve; select the latest available year and the 10-year column. Recalculate the 20-session change from this same official series: https://home.treasury.gov/resource-center/data-chart-center/interest-rates/TextView?type=daily_treasury_yield_curve
  • Direct EIA Cushing WTI daily spot-price history and download; do not replace spot with crude futures or a CFD: https://www.eia.gov/dnav/pet/hist/RWTCd.htm
  • Also check EIA Daily Prices for a newer completed WTI wholesale spot close: https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/prices.php. Use the date in “Wholesale Spot Petroleum Prices” (the close date), not the page publication date. Select WTI in USD/barrel; do not use the separate futures table. EIA republishes this spot quote from Refinitiv.
  • Direct Nasdaq Composite history; use final closing index levels: https://indexes.nasdaq.com/Index/History/COMP
  • Direct Nasdaq-100 history; match the S&P equity session: https://indexes.nasdaq.com/Index/History/NDX
  • Direct ICE MOVE data services; select end-of-day observations. If licensed access is unavailable, use Yahoo history below: https://developer.ice.com/fixed-income-data-services/catalog/ice-data-indices-move-index
  • Direct ICE fixed-income index services; require the exact ICE BofA US High Yield and BBB US Corporate option-adjusted-spread series. If unavailable, use their FRED series below: https://www.ice.com/fixed-income-data-services/index-solutions/fixed-income-indices
  • Direct Federal Reserve commercial paper daily rates; select 90-day AA financial and AA nonfinancial. An n.a. observation remains unavailable; use each CP rate and FRED DTB3 on its own latest verified observation date, even when the dates differ. Do not substitute another maturity, rating, or a Treasury investment/par yield for DTB3 discount-basis rates: https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/cp/rates.htm
  • VIX levels and daily history (Cboe): https://www.cboe.com/tradable_products/vix/vix_historical_data/
  • Cboe VIX daily CSV: https://cdn.cboe.com/api/global/us_indices/daily_prices/VIX_History.csv
  • Direct Cboe VIX3M daily closing history; subtract same-session VIX: https://cdn.cboe.com/api/global/us_indices/daily_prices/VIX3M_History.csv
  • VIX3M history; subtract same-session VIX for the term spread: https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/%5EVIX3M/history/
  • HY OAS, FRED BAMLH0A0HYM2: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/BAMLH0A0HYM2
  • BBB OAS, FRED BAMLC0A4CBBB: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/BAMLC0A4CBBB
  • 10-year Treasury yield: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DGS10
  • WTI Cushing spot price: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DCOILWTICO
  • S&P 500 OHLC and reported volume: https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/%5EGSPC/history/
  • Alternate Yahoo S&P 500 history page if the primary page has gaps: https://ca.finance.yahoo.com/quote/%5EGSPC/history/
  • Alternate Yahoo daily chart feeds when history pages are blocked or incomplete: https://query1.finance.yahoo.com/v8/finance/chart/%5EGSPC?range=2y&interval=1d and https://query2.finance.yahoo.com/v8/finance/chart/%5EGSPC?range=2y&interval=1d . Use the same encoded ticker on either host: %5EVIX, %5EVIX3M, %5EMOVE, JPY%3DX, %5EIXIC or %5ENDX as applicable. These are alternate access paths to the same provider, not independent confirmation. Inspect timestamps, exchange timezone, trading-period metadata and historical OHLC/volume; do not substitute a live metadata quote for a final historical close. A null daily record remains missing. Request enough history for every required window; a shorter request may diagnose a gap but cannot replace a 200-session window.
  • US bond-market holiday calendar: https://www.sifma.org/resources/general/holiday-schedule . Verify the year and applicable market before counting Treasury or credit-spread sessions.
  • Nasdaq Composite and Nasdaq 100 closing levels (same session as S&P 500): https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/NASDAQCOM and https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/NASDAQ100. Alternate: Yahoo ^IXIC and ^NDX history. Use index levels, not ETF prices.
  • Funding diagnostic: use the latest individually verified observation from each series: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DCPF3M , https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DCPN3M , https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DTB3 . Field 32 is the latest of the three observation dates (YYYYMMDD); fields 33–35 are the financial CP, nonfinancial CP and Treasury bill rates respectively. Append four numeric dates to the same line: field 36 equity session date, field 37 financial CP date, field 38 nonfinancial CP date, and field 39 Treasury bill date, all YYYYMMDD. The app automatically fills the four date boxes when Parse & Update is used. Dates may differ; do not invent rates or relabel an older rate with a newer date.
  • MOVE index history: https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/%5EMOVE/history/
  • USDJPY daily FX history: https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/JPY%3DX/history/
  • Breadth cross-checks: StockCharts $SPXA50R (S&P 500 percent above 50-day SMA), methodology: https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/trading-strategies-and-models/trading-strategies/percent-above-50-day-sma ; Barchart $S5FI: https://www.barchart.com/stocks/quotes/$S5FI . Require dated completed-session observations and accessible historical values. Providers may differ in constituent coverage and calculation conventions; investigate discrepancies rather than averaging them or selecting the newest/largest quote. Use one provider for both breadth endpoints, exactly 20 equity sessions apart. If switching providers, recompute both fields and disclose the switch. Sector charts are supplementary, not replacements.
  • Optional licensed equity-history alternative: Nasdaq Data Link End of Day S&P Index Prices, https://data.nasdaq.com/databases/BCIP . Use only with authorized access and verified instrument coverage, session convention and volume definition. It is not an automatic replacement for Yahoo ^GSPC reported volume; never splice another provider's volume into the Yahoo 20-session average.
  • S&P 500 breadth (select S&P 500 members, not all US stocks): https://www.thetrading.tools/market-breadth
  • Breadth history JSON; use spx_pct_above_50d and subtract its value 20 trading sessions earlier: https://www.thetrading.tools/data/market_breadth/market_breadth.json
  • FINRA margin debt table and historical Excel download: https://www.finra.org/rules-guidance/key-topics/margin-accounts/margin-statistics

Calculation checks: convert FRED credit-spread levels from percentage points to basis points by multiplying by 100. Calculate spread changes as differences in basis points. Calculate yield change as (latest yield − yield 20 trading sessions earlier) × 100. S&P distances are (close / simple moving average − 1) × 100 using 50 or 200 sessions including the signal session. VIX percentage changes use the specified trading-session lag. WTI uses the 20-published-observation rule below. Breadth change is a percentage-point difference from the same S&P 500 breadth series, not the all-US-stock series or a change in the index price. The suggested breadth provider uses current constituents; inspect its methodology. Use a consistent WTI spot-price series. S&P close, high, low and volume must refer to the same completed session; the volume average excludes that session. Do not replace missing observations with zero or shorten the averaging window.

WTI price and 20-observation change: Always use the newest verified published completed-day Cushing WTI spot price from EIA Daily Prices or EIA historical data, matching instrument, location, USD/barrel units and underlying Refinitiv source. WTI 20D % now means a 20-published-observation return, not an independently reconstructed trading-calendar return: sort unique dated non-missing daily observations chronologically, append a newer verified Daily Prices close once if needed, and calculate (newest price / price 20 observations earlier − 1) × 100. Use 21 dated observations including both endpoints. Count an unchanged value on a distinct date when the publisher reports it as a numeric daily observation, including holiday carry-forwards; do not require a separate spot-market holiday calendar. Ignore blank/n.a. observations and duplicate dates; never invent or fill prices. If a download is incomplete, try the alternate official history rather than treating download gaps as missing published observations. Update the price and recomputed change together. If the complete historical window remains unverifiable, retain the newest verified price and apply the best-estimate fallback to the change, disclosing endpoint evidence and any observation-count assumption; do not substitute an old change. This WTI-specific rule overrides the general session-calendar and older-group fallback rules; the explicitly labelled best-estimate exception still applies. State both endpoint dates, prices, source URLs and the 20-observation convention in the freshness note. Older saved WTI changes may use the previous trading-session convention; flag this methodology change when comparing trends.

Verified-data fallback when sources are delayed or unavailable: Look for the latest verifiable figures, using older observations where necessary. If a page is rate-limited, blocked, incomplete or showing an unfinished session, try the official CSV/JSON/Excel download or an alternate source. If accessible in your working environment, inspect previously saved source downloads (for this project, historical-data/) and their source dates. Do not assume an AI has access to local files. Use saved data only when its provenance, units, observation dates and completeness can be checked; do not treat dashboard sample values or a previous AI answer as verified source data.

Keep related inputs together: S&P close, high, low and reported ^GSPC volume must match one completed session, with low ≤ close ≤ high. Calculate its daily return, 50/200-session moving-average distances and preceding 20-session volume average relative to that same session, using every required session. Match both Nasdaq closes to that equity session. Keep each other level and its changes anchored to the same observation date and series: VIX and its changes plus same-date VIX3M spread; HY OAS and its changes; Treasury yield and its change; WTI spot and its change; S&P breadth and its change; USDJPY close and its 3-FX-session change. If a required history window has gaps, find a complete source and apply the newest-data rule above. Keep the newest verified level; apply the best-estimate fallback to an unresolved derived metric and identify it outside the numeric line. Never shorten a window, reuse an older change for a newer endpoint, or fill a gap with zero.

Check FINRA's current published table for a newer report even if saved downloads contain an older month. Publication delays and insufficient-trade CP observations cannot be filled using estimates or another website's live proxy. Use that published reference month, debt in USD millions, and the same series 12 and 3 months earlier. Keep each CP/Treasury rate on its own latest verified observation date. Field 32 records the latest of these three dates, not a claim that all rates share that date. Include the three individual funding dates in fields 37–39 and the equity session date in field 36; field 32 must equal the latest of fields 37–39. Different indicator groups may use different dates because publication schedules differ; do not describe the resulting row as a single-session snapshot.

The app derives CP scoring and Nasdaq 20-matched-observation relative momentum from these 35 raw fields and verified stored history. Do not append a computed score or momentum field. Missing historical windows remain unknown in the 50-point model.

Output format: the data line must contain exactly 39 numeric values separated by 38 commas, with no blank fields, missing-value placeholders, thousands separators, headings, Markdown fences, explanations or citations inside that line. Always give a compact source-verification table before the numeric line, covering every indicator group with provider/series, plain source URL, observation date or reference month, verification status and required comparison endpoints or average-window dates. Include a short freshness note for older observations or saved-download fallbacks. Briefly distinguish publication delays, access failures, missing sessions, unfinished sessions, rejected inconsistent data and unresolved instrument identity; state why each older date was used and disclose material revisions. Do not call mixed-date inputs a single-session snapshot. Include all four dates as numeric YYYYMMDD values in fields 36–39, even when dates match. Never use the retrieval date in place of an observation date. Then put the paste-ready numeric line on its own line; only that numeric line goes into the 39-value text box. Keep this source-verification table outside the paste-ready line. If some values remain unverified, provide the complete 39-number row using defensible best estimates, preceded by the provisional label and field-by-field assumptions. Withhold the row only if a field has no defensible numerical basis; never fabricate a number to meet the count.

Field 36 automatically fills this box when you select Parse & Update. Use the actual equity session date, not today’s paste date.

CP and Treasury observation dates

Fields 37–39 automatically fill these boxes when you select Parse & Update. The dates may differ. For a 35-field paste, enter the dates manually; blank boxes use field 32 for all three rates only when they actually share a date.

Current and past entries

Saved when you select Parse & Update; edit saved dates and numbers directly in this table. Newest entry first. Use the red × to delete a row after confirmation. Deleting the current saved entry restores the latest remaining entry, or sample defaults if none remain. Edit a saved row’s date, time or indicator values, then select Save. Its composite score is calculated from the existing market indicators plus margin leverage, volume pressure, CP funding stress and Nasdaq relative momentum (50 points maximum). Changing the entry date or time preserves its indicator values; edit value cells explicitly to change them. Rows are reordered by date; the newest saved row supplies the current dashboard values. Unavailable added inputs display as a score range, never as assumed zero. Dates default to entry time and can be changed to your observation time, in , not when the market data was published. Units appear in column headings; value cells contain numbers only.

Forced Selling and Funding Diagnostics

Risk Factors for Force Selling

Dollar funding stress · diagnostic only

What this USD amount represents: SWPT measures the Federal Reserve’s aggregate outstanding US-dollar liquidity swaps with foreign central banks—a form of dollar lending through central-bank swap lines. Those central banks can lend the dollars onward to institutions in their jurisdictions and remain responsible for repayment to the Federal Reserve. The figure is the balance outstanding on each Wednesday, in USD millions, rather than the amount newly lent during that week.

Whose account is it? This is an aggregate Federal Reserve balance-sheet item.

Tracking dollar funding stress can help identify institutional liquidity shortages that may increase the risk of asset sales and wider market disruption.

When short-term dollar borrowing becomes unavailable or expensive, institutions still facing margin calls or cash obligations may need to sell assets, draw reserves or obtain other funding.

  • Indiscriminate selling: Under severe funding pressure, investors may sell liquid holdings—including stocks, gold and corporate debt—because buyers are available, even when those assets’ fundamentals have not deteriorated.
  • The signal: Funding indicators can flag conditions associated with forced selling. They do not establish that such selling or a crash is imminent; weekly swap balances also reflect liquidity support intended to ease pressure.

Fed central-bank liquidity swaps (SWPT), USD millions. Weekly outstanding balances are not gross drawdowns or proof of yen-carry liquidation. No contribution to the 50-point score. White figures are informational, not a low-risk classification.

Commercial-Paper (CP) Funding & Leadership

Funding spreads & market leadership · scored inputs and diagnostic watches

CP Diagnostic Alerts

Short-term funding costs and relative equity performance add context to the Credit and Equity regimes. The CP spread component contributes up to 3 Credit points and Nasdaq relative momentum contributes up to 3 Equity points to the 50-point score. Percentile-based watch alerts remain separate from those fixed scoring thresholds. White numbers are informational, not a low-risk label.

Commercial-paper spreads compare 90-day AA financial and nonfinancial borrowing rates. A rising financial premium can suggest funding pressure, but a small difference can conceal stress affecting both groups. Spreads over 3-month Treasury bills provide a second reference; Treasury demand, issuer composition and liquidity also affect them. These are discount-basis yield differences, not FRA–OIS or pure default-risk measures.

Sources: Financial CP · Nonfinancial CP · Treasury bills · Federal Reserve methodology. Embedded source downloaded September 25, 2026. Historical source charts use same-date observations. AI-assisted updates also accept separately verified dates per rate; mixed-date scoring is labelled and does not replace same-date source history. This downloaded vintage is retrospective and must not be treated as a point-in-time backtest. Quick Paste includes the CP rates and separate observation dates. Saving a paste, editing history or loading account data refreshes these diagnostics automatically. Saved rates override embedded rates for their stated observation date; older pastes leave funding data unchanged. Account sync transfers saved inputs; it does not fetch market data.

Debt and cash-flow checks: Commercial paper is short-term borrowing used by financial firms and other large companies to meet funding needs. The first three alerts compare those borrowing costs with each other and with US Treasury bills. Rising premiums can indicate funding pressure; a disruption can affect refinancing and markets, but does not by itself establish that a systemic crash will follow.

This selector follows the other current charts. Historical study periods keep their fixed dates. Each graph shows one diagnostic plus S&P 500 (green), Nasdaq Composite (purple dashed) and Nasdaq 100 (gold dotted). Equity indexes share the right-hand scale, rebased to 100 on the first common session; diagnostic values use the left-hand scale.

Financial minus nonfinancial CP · basis points

Compares 90-day AA borrowing rates for financial firms, including banks, with those for nonfinancial companies. A widening positive spread means financial firms face a larger borrowing premium relative to the corporate comparison group.

Blue line · Relative funding cost of AA financial issuers versus AA nonfinancial issuers.

Financial CP minus Treasury bills · basis points

Compares financial firms’ 90-day AA borrowing rates with 3-month US Treasury bill rates. A wider spread can reflect greater credit or liquidity concerns, as well as stronger demand for Treasury bills.

Purple line · Financial funding premium over 3-month Treasury bills.

Nonfinancial CP minus Treasury bills · basis points

Compares nonfinancial companies’ 90-day AA borrowing rates with 3-month US Treasury bill rates. A widening spread can indicate more expensive short-term corporate funding relative to the government benchmark.

Teal line · Nonfinancial funding premium over 3-month Treasury bills. Gaps mean missing data; Scoring thresholds are heuristic and have not been calibrated.

Nasdaq 100 / S&P 500 · 20-matched-observation relative momentum

The market-leadership check asks whether the technology-heavy Nasdaq 100 is losing strength relative to the broader S&P 500. Nasdaq 100 is not exclusively a technology index. Increasing underperformance can flag changing leadership or pressure on growth stocks, but does not confirm forced selling. Both indexes can fall even while Nasdaq outperforms.

100 × [(Nasdaq 100 / S&P 500) today ÷ the ratio 20 matched observations earlier − 1]. Positive means Nasdaq 100 outperformance; negative means underperformance. This measures market leadership, not a pure technology/value rotation, fund flows or forced selling. Uses price indexes, excluding dividends, and the latest 21 distinct dates with valid closes for both indexes. Missing pairs are skipped, so the window can span more than 20 trading sessions. Quick Paste equity closes feed the calculation. Fewer than 21 matched observations leave the result unavailable. Scoring thresholds are unchanged; comparisons with older consecutive-session scores may reflect the changed window.

Methodology and Indicators

Indicators Explained

D means trading days; DMA means daily moving average; bp means basis points (100 bp = 1 percentage point); pp means percentage points.

IndicatorUnitExplanation
10Y 20D bp changebpChange in 10-year Treasury yield over twenty trading days. A move from 4.50% to 4.80% is 30 basis points.
10Y Yield%Yield on the 10-year US Treasury. Enter 4.80 for 4.80%. This dashboard assigns more risk points to higher yields.
200DMA distance velocity5-session change in ppToday’s S&P percentage distance from its own 200DMA minus the distance 5 equity sessions earlier. Each moving average uses only information then available. Below the 200DMA, a loss of 3 pp flags watch and 5 pp flags stress. Not proof of forced liquidation and not extra points.
BBB OASbpOption-adjusted spread for BBB-rated investment-grade corporate bonds. Higher readings indicate more credit risk priced into these bonds.
Breadth % >50DMA%Percentage of S&P 500 constituents above their own 50-day moving averages. Lower values indicate fewer stocks participating in the uptrend.
Breadth 20D changeppCurrent breadth minus its value 20 trading sessions earlier, in percentage points. Loss ≤−10 pp: 2 points. Otherwise, loss ≤−4 pp with current breadth <65%: 1 point; otherwise 0. This flags deteriorating participation even before an index breaks its trend.
Commercial-paper funding stressbp · 0–3 pointsCompare same-date financial minus nonfinancial CP and financial CP minus Treasury bills. Either spread ≥25/50 bp respectively: 2 points; ≥50/100 bp: 3 instead. Rates older than seven calendar days still determine the CP score, with a stale-data note. Missing, invalid or future-dated rates give a 0–3 range. Credit category maximum: 14.
Financial / nonfinancial CP spreadsbpSame-date 90-day AA financial minus nonfinancial CP rate × 100; also compare each to 3-month Treasury bills. Diagnostic only. Missing rates are not carried forward. Small sector differences do not rule out broad funding stress.
HY OAS 20D bp changebpCurrent high-yield OAS minus its value twenty trading days ago. Positive values mean spreads widened.
HY OAS 5D bp changebpCurrent high-yield OAS minus its value five trading days ago. Positive values mean spreads widened.
HY OASbpHigh-yield corporate bond option-adjusted spread over a Treasury benchmark, adjusted for embedded options. Wider spreads indicate greater credit stress.
Margin debt / reference monthUSD million / YYYYMMAggregate customer securities-margin debit balances from FINRA. Monthly, not daily; use a published report or the explicitly assumed two-month lag for historical data.
Margin debt YoY / 3M change%(Current debt / debt 12 or 3 months earlier − 1) × 100. Leverage points: maximum of YoY ≥20% → 1, ≥40% → 2; 3M ≤−5% → 1, ≤−10% → 2. Maximum 2, not the sum.
Margin leverage0–2 pointsUses FINRA customer margin debt. Buildup: year-over-year growth ≥20% earns 1 point; ≥40% earns 2. Deleveraging: three-month change ≤−5% earns 1; ≤−10% earns 2. Take the higher score, not their sum. Monthly debt does not measure total financial-system leverage. The reference month and debt amount inherit this component’s color; the date or dollar amount alone has no risk threshold.
Market leadership momentum20-matched-observation %100 × [(Nasdaq 100 / S&P 500) today / the ratio 20 sessions earlier − 1]. Negative means Nasdaq 100 underperformance; not evidence of fund flows or forced liquidation. Requires all 21 sessions, contributes no score.
MOVEIndexICE BofA bond-market implied-volatility index based on US Treasury options. Higher values indicate greater expected interest-rate volatility.
Nasdaq 100 closeIndexClosing level of the Nasdaq 100, tracking large non-financial Nasdaq-listed companies. Monitoring only; no added score.
Nasdaq Composite closeIndexClosing level of the broad Nasdaq Composite. Use the index, not an ETF. Monitoring only; no added score. Both Nasdaq chart lines are rebased to 100 for comparison with the S&P 500.
Nasdaq relative momentum scoring20-matched-observation % · 0–3 points100 × [(Nasdaq 100 / S&P 500) ÷ the ratio 20 matched observations earlier − 1]. ≤−3%: 1 point; ≤−6%: 3. Requires all 21 sessions; unavailable history gives 0–3. Equity category maximum: 12. Relative weakness is not proof of liquidation.
Possible volume exhaustionObservationAt least 2× volume, a new 20-session low, close above the open and in the top 30% of the day’s range. A possible reversal, not a confirmed bottom; adds no separate points.
Reported volume / prior 20D averageSharesYahoo ^GSPC reported-volume proxy. Average the preceding 20 trading sessions, excluding the signal day. Keep the same provider and units.
S&P 500 session high / lowIndex pointsSame-session high and low matching the closing index level. Close location = (close − low) / (high − low). Location ≤0.25 activates selling-volume scoring even on an up day. Missing, invalid or zero-width ranges stay unknown; negative daily returns can still establish selling pressure independently.
S&P vs 200DMA%S&P 500 distance from its 200-day moving average, using the same formula. Negative values indicate weakness versus the longer-term trend.
S&P vs 50DMA%S&P 500 distance from its 50-day moving average: (index / average − 1) × 100. Negative values mean the index is below its average.
S&P 500 daily change%(Current closing level / previous trading-session close − 1) × 100. Used to distinguish selling volume from rising-price volume.
Selling volume0–2 pointsDivide reported S&P volume by the average of the preceding 20 trading sessions, excluding the current day. If the S&P closes below its previous session OR closes in the bottom 25% of its session range: ratio ≥1.5 earns 1 point; ≥2 earns 2. Otherwise 0. Volume, average volume and daily return inherit this component’s color. Heavy volume alone does not confirm forced selling or a market bottom.
USDJPY carry-trade stress3-session % change · 0–2 points(Current USDJPY / close 3 FX trading sessions earlier − 1) × 100. Above −1.5%: 0 points; −1.5% to above −3%: 1; −3% or lower: 2. Yen appreciation means negative USDJPY change. Absolute exchange-rate levels no longer score. This is a heuristic warning of possible carry unwinds, not proof of liquidation or a validated forecast.
USDJPY momentum diagnostic% over 3 FX sessions(USDJPY / value 3 available FX observations earlier − 1) × 100. Negative means yen appreciation. Amber at −1.5%, red at −3%. Replaces the former absolute-level currency score, maximum 2 points.
USDJPYJPY/USDJapanese yen per US dollar, shown for reference. Currency risk points use the separate three-session percentage change; absolute exchange-rate levels do not score.
VIX 1D %%Percentage change in VIX from the previous trading day: (current / previous − 1) × 100. This is not the separate VIX1D index.
VIX 3M-1M spreadIndex pointsVIX3M minus 30-day VIX, in index points; these are implied-volatility indices, not front-month futures. Negative spread: 2 points. A nonnegative spread <1.0 with VIX 5D change >10% also earns 2. Otherwise spread <1.5 earns 1; ≥1.5 earns 0. Zero is flat, not backwardation. This measures a narrow curve, not its rate of flattening; both inputs should be from the same closing session.
VIX 5D %%Percentage change in VIX over five trading days. A positive value means expected volatility has risen.
VIXIndexExpected annualized S&P 500 volatility over the next 30 days, derived from options prices. Higher readings indicate greater expected movement, not its direction.
Volume ratio / selling pressureRatio / 0–2 pointsVolume divided by prior 20D average. On a negative S&P daily return or a close in the bottom 25% of the session range: ratio ≥1.5 adds 1 point; ≥2 adds 2. Otherwise 0. Missing inputs produce a score range.
WTI 20D %%Percentage change from the newest verified published Cushing WTI spot price to 20 published daily observations earlier. Count distinct numeric dates, including unchanged holiday carry-forwards; omit blank observations. This replaces the former trading-session convention for new updates; historical saved values are not recalculated.
WTIUSD/barrelWest Texas Intermediate crude oil price. Use the same spot or futures series for all entries and its 20-day change. This dashboard flags high oil prices as a macro stress signal.

S&P 500 close: the closing level of the S&P 500 price index; shown for comparison and excluded from the risk score. Context: Cboe implied-volatility term structure · Federal Reserve: borrowing costs and economic activity. Reference definitions: Cboe volatility indices · ICE MOVE · ICE bond methodology. Risk colors follow this dashboard’s existing scoring rules.

50-point scoring model

Volatility 10 + Credit 14 + Macro 8 + Equity Structure 12 + Forced Selling 6 = 50. Current entries, saved history and all historical studies recalculate from their underlying inputs using the same model. The first 35 Quick Paste fields retain their order; fields 36–39 supply the four observation dates.

1. Commercial-paper funding stress: 0, 2 or 3 Credit points

Financial CP minus nonfinancial CP measures financial firms’ borrowing premium relative to other corporations. Financial CP minus Treasury bills measures their premium relative to the government benchmark.

Spread in bp = (rate A − rate B) × 100; input rates are percentages.

ConditionAdded Credit points
Financial–nonfinancial below 25 bp AND financial–Treasury below 50 bp0
Financial–nonfinancial ≥25 bp OR financial–Treasury ≥50 bp2
Financial–nonfinancial ≥50 bp OR financial–Treasury ≥100 bp3

The higher threshold replaces the lower one. The app never adds 2 + 3 or sums the two spreads’ scores; there is no 1-point tier. For example, financial CP 4.07%, nonfinancial CP 4.08% and Treasury bills 4.02% give −1 bp and 5 bp: 0 added points; show a stale-data warning if the common observation is more than seven calendar days old.

All three rates must share a verified date on or before the scored entry date. Data more than seven calendar days old remains usable for scoring with an explicit stale-data warning. Missing, invalid or future-dated inputs produce 0–3 unknown points. Seven days is a freshness convention, not a validated financial threshold.

2. Nasdaq-100 relative momentum: 0, 1 or 3 Equity Structure points

Momentum % = [(Nasdaq 100 / S&P 500 today) ÷ (Nasdaq 100 / S&P 500 20 matched observations earlier) − 1] × 100

Relative momentumAdded Equity Structure points
Above −3%0
−3% to above −6%1
−6% or lower3

There is no 2-point tier. A ratio falling from 4.00 to 3.76 changes by −6%, adding 3 points. This measures relative underperformance: both indexes can fall without triggering it, or Nasdaq can rise but lag enough to trigger it. The Nasdaq Composite remains a comparison index and earns no points.

The latest 21 matched session observations are used, skipping dates missing either index. The baseline is 20 matched observations before the endpoint and may be more than 20 trading sessions earlier. Fewer than 21 matched observations gives a 0–3 range, never an invented baseline. Historical nontrading dates use their recorded trading-session snapshot. Mixed-date pasted prices remain a limitation.

Score bands: 0–4 Normal Risk; 5–9 Correction Risk; 10–15 Systemic Stress; 16–22 High Stress; 23–30 High Risk; 31–50 Systemic Risk. Thresholds are heuristics, not validated crash probabilities. Historical calculations use downloaded data vintages, not publication-time backtests. Dollar swaps, 200DMA velocity and percentile watch alerts remain unscored.

Sources: Federal Reserve CP methodology, Nasdaq-100 via FRED. FRA–OIS thresholds are not carried over following the LIBOR transition.

Advanced Systemic Crash Risk Dashboard Explained

Explanatory reference. The illustrative thresholds below do not replace the dashboard’s scoring rules in the Risk Factor Table.

Five primary regimes

The framework categorizes risk into five primary regimes, tracking specific mechanisms and triggers:

  • 🌪️ Volatility Regime: Covers the VIX (measuring 30-day implied equity volatility, elevated >20), VIX 1D % and 5D % (tracking sudden and sustained volatility acceleration), VIX 3M-1M Spread (measuring curve inversion <0.0), and the MOVE Index (tracking fixed-income instability >100–110).
  • 💳 Credit Regime: Focuses on HY OAS (junk bond spreads widening >350 bp) alongside 5D and 20D changes for short- and long-term credit freezes, plus BBB OAS monitoring investment-grade stress.
  • ⚡ Macro Shock: Monitors the 10Y Yield and its 20D velocity changes (spikes >4.5% and >15 bp), alongside WTI Crude absolute prices and 20D momentum (>$90/bbl and >10%).
  • 📐 Equity Structure: Evaluates technical health via S&P vs 50DMA and 200DMA distance (<0%), as well as Breadth % >50DMA participation and its 20D momentum decay.
  • 🌊 Forced Selling: Tracks the USDJPY 3-Session % (rapid Yen surges ≤-1.5%) to signal carry trade unwinding.

🔍 Secondary Risk Filters (Structural Context)

Additional systemic amplifiers evaluated for selling pressure severity include:

  • FINRA Margin Debt: Tracks leverage expansion (YoY ≥ 40%) for bubbles and contraction (3M ≤ -10%) for liquidations.
  • S&P 500 Volume Ratio: Compares volume against the 20-day average ( ≥ 1.5–2.0) with negative returns to signal institutional liquidation.
Risk Factor🔄 Normal Market Conditions🚨 Crash Mechanism & Systemic Triggers
💳 Credit Spreads (HY OAS & BBB OAS)Tight Spreads: HY OAS hovers between 250–450 bp; BBB sits near 100 bp. Tight spreads can reflect confidence in credit conditions, though defaults remain possible.Credit Crunch: HY OAS widens aggressively past 400–500 bp (alongside spiking 5D/20D deltas). Widening spreads may reflect higher perceived credit or liquidity risk and can raise refinancing costs.
💰 FINRA Margin Debt (YoY % & 3M Change %)Controlled Leverage: Moderate growth tracks expanding asset values. Leverage acts as an efficient amplifier of capital efficiency across retail and institutional brokerages.Forced Deleveraging: YoY growth hits extreme peaks (≥ 40%) suggesting elevated leverage, or a sharp 3M contraction (≤ -10%). A drop may be consistent with deleveraging, but monthly aggregates do not identify individual margin calls or establish their cause.
🌾 Market Breadth (% > 50DMA & 20D Change)Broad Participation: > 65% of individual stocks trade above their 50DMAs. The broader index advance is driven by health across multiple underlying sectors, rather than just a few mega-caps.Internal Decay: Breadth collapses < 40% or drops sharply over 20 sessions (≤ -10 pp). The index may look stable on the surface, but fewer constituents may be sustaining the uptrend, suggesting weaker participation.
📈 MOVE Index (Bond Market Volatility)Stable Funding: Sits below 80–90. Treasury yields move predictably, allowing commercial banks, mortgage providers, and institutional desks to price and hedge fixed-income assets safely.Liquidity Freeze: Index spikes above 100–110. Large yield fluctuations can complicate hedging and may coincide with wider bid-ask spreads or reduced liquidity.
🛒 S&P 500 Volume Ratio (Session vs 20D Average)Institutional Balance: Volume mirrors the trailing 20-day average (~1.0x). Capital flows cleanly between buyers and sellers without causing disruptive intraday gaps.Institutional Capitulation: Volume surges past 1.5x–2.0x the average while the index closes down or in the bottom quarter of its daily range. This can indicate elevated selling pressure, but does not identify the sellers or confirm a capitulation bottom.
📐 Trend Distances (S&P vs 50DMA & 200DMA)Bullish Structure: S&P 500 trades above both lines (+3% to +10%). Trading above these averages is consistent with a positive trend, but neither average guarantees support during a pullback.Technical Breakdown: S&P plunges below both averages (< 0%). A break below the 200DMA may prompt some trend-following strategies to reduce exposure; their actual trading cannot be established from this indicator alone.
🌊 USD/JPY Carry Trade (3-Session % Change)Stable Carry: Exchange rates remain steady or grind slowly higher. Macro investors may borrow yen to invest in higher-yielding global assets (like U.S. equities and tech debt).The Unwind: USD/JPY drops rapidly (≤ -1.5% to -3% across 3 days). A strengthening yen can put pressure on yen-funded positions and may lead some investors to reduce exposure; the currency move alone does not prove forced liquidation.
🌪️ VIX & Volatility Acceleration (VIX Level, VIX 1D %, VIX 5D %)Suppressed / Mean-Reverting: VIX sits between 12–18. Daily fluctuations reflect standard noise or expected earnings adjustments without persistent directional momentum.The Shock: VIX spikes above 20–25 with rapid 1D and 5D acceleration (>10%). This can indicate increased demand for protection and heightened near-term uncertainty; it does not establish institutional panic or a continuing decline.
📉 VIX 3M–1M Spread (Volatility Term Structure)Contango: The spread is positive. Investors naturally demand a higher premium to insure against stock market turbulence over a longer 90-day horizon (VIX3M) than a short 30-day horizon (VIX).Backwardation: The spread turns negative (< 0). Investors aggressively bid up immediate, front-month protective options to shield portfolios right now, indicating greater near-term uncertainty rather than establishing that a crash is imminent.
🛢️ WTI Crude Oil (Absolute & 20D Velocity)Equilibrium Price: Prices remain aligned with stable global industrial demand, keeping supply chains profitable without triggering consumer wallet tightening.Stagflationary Spike: WTI surges past $90/bbl with rapid 20D momentum (>10%). Spiking energy costs act as an immediate tax on global economic output, potentially adding inflation pressure and complicating monetary-policy decisions.
⚡ 10Y Treasury Yield (Absolute & 20D Velocity)Balanced Macro: Yields trade within established macroeconomic ranges matching steady growth and moderate, controlled inflation targets.Rate Shock: Yields spike vertically (20D change > +15–30 bp). Rapid yield increases can reduce existing bond prices, pressure equity valuations through discount rates, and increase financing strain for leveraged borrowers.

📉 1. The VIX 3M–1M Spread (Volatility Term Structure)

The VIX measures expected stock market volatility over the next 30 days (1 month), while the VIX3M measures expected volatility over the next 90 days (3 months).

🔄 Normal Market Conditions (Contango)

In many calmer periods, the spread is positive (VIX3M is higher than the VIX). This is because the future is inherently uncertain. Investors naturally demand a higher premium to insure against stock market turbulence over a longer 90-day horizon than a short 30-day horizon.

🚨 Crash Mechanism: Curve Inversion (Backwardation)

When VIX exceeds VIX3M, the spread is negative. This inversion is consistent with greater implied volatility over the near-term horizon and can accompany increased demand for immediate protection.

  • The Signal: A negative spread indicates higher near-term than three-month implied volatility; it does not establish a particular future event.
  • Why it Matters: Persistent inversion can be a useful stress signal to assess alongside credit and breadth, but does not establish an imminent crash.

💳 2. High-Yield Option-Adjusted Spread (HY OAS)

The HY OAS measures the additional interest rate yield that "junk bonds" (riskier corporate debt) must pay over risk-free U.S. Treasuries, mathematically adjusted to remove the distortions of embedded options (like a company's right to call back debt early).

🔄 Normal Market Conditions

During stronger economic conditions, perceived corporate default risk may decline. Investors are comfortable holding lower-rated corporate debt, causing high-yield spreads to compress and sit tight against Treasuries (often between 250 to 350 basis points).

🚨 Crash Mechanism: The Credit Squeeze

Credit spreads can reflect changing expectations about defaults, liquidity and risk appetite. They sometimes deteriorate ahead of equities, but do not reliably lead every downturn.

  • The Signal: A shift away from high-yield debt can reduce its prices and raise yields relative to Treasuries. The HY OAS may widen, reflecting changing credit and liquidity conditions.
  • Why it Matters: A rapid widening in HY OAS (for example, beyond 400–500 basis points) can indicate greater credit or liquidity stress. More expensive refinancing can pressure vulnerable companies and equity valuations, but does not establish a liquidity freeze or make bankruptcies and falling stock prices inevitable.

📐 3. Mathematical Formula: 200DMA Distance Velocity

The 200DMA Distance Velocity and Forced Selling components help the dashboard identify structural market stress and potential selling pressure. The mathematical and scoring logic is explained below.

200DMA Distance Velocity is a contextual diagnostic and adds no points. The Forced Selling category contributes up to 6 points to the 50-point total.

This metric isolates the momentum of trend decay—how quickly the index moves relative to its long-term anchor—rather than looking only at the absolute price level. It requires two calculations.

Step 1: Calculate the percentage distance from the 200DMA

For trading session t, the percentage distance Dt is the S&P 500 closing price Pt divided by its 200-day simple moving average, minus 1, multiplied by 100.

Dt = (Pt / SMA200,t − 1) × 100

The 200-day simple moving average includes the current session’s closing price.

Step 2: Calculate velocity over five equity trading sessions

Velocity Vt is the percentage-point difference between the current distance and the distance exactly five equity trading sessions earlier.

Vt = Dt − Dt−5

🚨 Stress triggers

These warnings apply only while the S&P 500 is below its 200-day moving average (Dt < 0%).

  • Watch: Velocity ≤ −3 percentage points over five sessions.
  • Stress: Velocity ≤ −5 percentage points over five sessions, indicating a faster deterioration in the index’s position relative to its trend.

🌊 4. Exact Scoring Bounds: Forced Selling Category

The Forced Selling category has a maximum of 6 points within the dashboard’s 50-point total. It combines USDJPY carry-trade stress, FINRA margin leverage, and volume selling pressure.

A. USDJPY carry-trade stress · maximum 2 points

This component measures the percentage change in USDJPY over three FX trading sessions. A negative change means the yen has strengthened against the dollar.

  • 0 points: Change > −1.5%.
  • 1 point · amber: Change ≤ −1.5% and > −3.0%, indicating rapid yen appreciation and potential pressure on carry trades.
  • 2 points · red: Change ≤ −3.0%, indicating a more severe yen surge and potential pressure to reduce positions financed in yen.

B. FINRA margin leverage · maximum 2 points

This component evaluates monthly FINRA margin debt using year-over-year growth and the three-month change. It takes the higher of the two scores; the scores are not added together.

Measure0 points1 point · amber2 points · red
Leverage buildup · YoY change< 20%≥ 20% and < 40%≥ 40%
Deleveraging · three-month change> −5%≤ −5% and > −10%≤ −10%

C. Volume selling pressure · maximum 2 points

The volume ratio compares current-session reported S&P 500 volume with the average of the preceding 20 sessions, excluding the current session.

Rvol = reported session volume / prior 20-session average volume

Points apply only when at least one of these conditions is met:

  1. The S&P 500 daily closing return is negative (< 0%).
  2. The S&P 500 closes in the bottom 25% of its daily high–low range.

When either condition is met, the volume thresholds are:

  • 0 points: Volume ratio < 1.5.
  • 1 point · amber: Volume ratio ≥ 1.5 and < 2.0.
  • 2 points · red: Volume ratio ≥ 2.0.

These are heuristic pressure signals, not proof of institutional liquidation or a confirmed market bottom. Missing inputs produce score ranges rather than assumed zero risk.
